extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students studying complex analysis (and contest/qual prep students)
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and criteria for holomorphic and meromorphic functions, poles/residues, contour integrals (residue theorem and argument principle), and existence conditions for holomorphic roots and logarithms. Includes examples, exercises, and topological lifting criteria used to decide branch existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus for path integrals / antiderivative construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the antiderivative F : Ω → C by integrating f across the side of a rectangle, prove F ′ = f, and get a “fundamental theorem of calculus” stating ∮_α f(z) dz = F(α(b)) − F(α(a)) for a path α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: for a loop γ, since start and end points coincide, the contour integral is 0. This construction is used to extend contour integral results to arbitrary curves (even those without interior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ML-estimate in vanishing integral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing integrals over a sequence of shrinking curves (rectangles γ_j) one can bound integrals using the M·L estimation lemma to show the integrals tend to zero at a rate tied to curve length and sup-norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 31.7.4: finish the proof using the M L estimation lemma — keep track of magnitudes (not just nonzero) because integral sizes scale differently from perimeters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liouville's theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : C → C be an entire function. Suppose that |f(z)| < 1000 for all complex numbers z. Prove that f is a constant function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical application: bounded entire functions must be constant; used often to deduce impossibility of nonconstant bounded holomorphic maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeros are isolated (zeros-of-holomorphic-functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The zero set of any nonzero holomorphic function f : U → C is an isolated set, unless there exists a nonempty open subset of U on which f is identically zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: isolated set means around each point in S one can draw a neighborhood not intersecting any other point of S. This underpins Laurent/Taylor expansions at zeros/poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f, g : U → C be holomorphic, and assume that U is connected. Prove that if f and g agree on some open neighborhood, then f = g on U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show uniqueness of analytic continuations and uniqueness of Laurent/Taylor expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum modulus principle (maximums occur on boundaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : U → C be holomorphic, let Y ⊆ U be compact, and let ∂Y be boundary of Y. Show that max_{z∈Y} |f(z)| = max_{z∈∂Y} |f(z)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: nonconstant holomorphic functions cannot attain a strict interior maximum of modulus; existence of maxima on compact sets follows from continuity and compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removable singularity theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let U be open, p ∈ U, and f : U \ {p} → C be holomorphic. Suppose f is bounded. Show that lim_{z→p} f(z) exists, and the extension f : U → C is holomorphic at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boundedness near an isolated singularity implies the singularity is removable; extend f by the limit value to restore holomorphicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: meromorphic function (quotient form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : U → C is meromorphic if there exists holomorphic functions A, B : U → C with B not identically zero in any open neighborhood, and f(z) = A(z)/B(z) whenever B(z) ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the concrete, algebraic definition analogous to rational functions; example: 1/z is meromorphic on C with pole at 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate definition: meromorphic via isolated poles and Laurent series
rubrics_metrics.description: A meromorphic function is holomorphic on U except at an isolated set S of points; for each p ∈ S, f admits a Laurent series with finite principal part c_{-m}/(z−p)^m + … + c_{-1}/(z−p) + c_0 + c_1(z−p) + … with c_{-m} ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolated poles means we can choose pairwise-disjoint neighborhoods around each pole. This characterization is equivalent to the quotient form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pole order and residue
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has Laurent expansion at p with leading negative-power term c_{-m}/(z−p)^m then m is the order of the pole (simple pole if m=1) and c_{-1} is the residue Res(f; p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order measures how 'bad' the pole is (analogy: negative zero multiplicity). Examples and computations show how residues and orders behave under multiplication/division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orders are additive under multiplication/division
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has a pole/zero of order k at a point and g has order ℓ, then f·g has order k+ℓ; e.g., multiplying Laurent/Taylor series shows orders add. Consequently, dividing can reduce order additionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 32.2.7: convince yourself of this by examining Taylor/Laurent series; used in computing poles of rational meromorphic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laurent series uniqueness and principal/analytic parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Laurent series, if it exists, is unique; the negative-power part c_{-m}/(z−p)^m + … + c_{-1}/(z−p) is the principal part and the rest is the analytic part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniqueness follows from analytic continuation/identity theorem; principal part encodes the singular behavior and residue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winding number definition and basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For a point p ∈ C and a loop γ not passing through it, define I(γ,p) = (1/(2πi)) ∮_γ 1/(z−p) dz. The winding number is always an integer; for a circle counterclockwise it's 1 if p inside and 0 if outside. A loop is regular if I(γ,p)=1 for all points p in the interior of γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winding number measures how many times γ winds around p; it generalizes inside/outside counts and is crucial in the residue theorem formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's residue theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : Ω → C be meromorphic on simply connected Ω. For any loop γ not passing through poles, (1/(2πi)) ∮_γ f(z) dz = Σ_{p pole} I(γ,p) Res(f; p). In particular for a regular γ, the integral equals the sum of residues of poles inside γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: decompose f into holomorphic part g and principal parts at poles; integral of g vanishes by Cauchy-Goursat; each principal part contributes its residue times winding number. Used to compute integrals and coefficients in Laurent series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy integral formula intuition via residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrating f(z)/(z−a) around boundary of a disk picks out the c_0 coefficient (f(a)) in the Laurent expansion at a; more generally residues extract coefficients corresponding to (z−a)^{-1} terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate f to move desired coefficient to the (z−a)^{-1} slot (e.g., divide by z−a) and apply residue theorem to recover function values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logarithmic derivative is meromorphic and residue characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: For meromorphic f, f'/f is meromorphic; its only poles are at zeros and poles of f. At a zero of multiplicity k the residue equals k, and at a pole of order k the residue equals −k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute via Laurent expansion: if f(z)=c_k z^k + … then f'/f has simple pole with residue equal to exponent k. This is key to turning zeros/poles into residues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Let γ be a regular curve and f meromorphic inside/on γ with no zeros/poles on γ. Then (1/(2πi)) ∮_γ f'/f dz = Z − P, where Z is number of zeros inside γ (counted with multiplicity) and P is number of poles inside γ (with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from residue theorem plus logarithmic derivative proposition. Generalizes via winding numbers: sum I(γ,z) over zeros minus sum I(γ,p) over poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological lifting criterion for holomorphic roots (covering map condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of a holomorphic nth root for f amounts to existence of a lifting of f|_V through the covering projection p(w)=w^n : E=C\{0} → B=C\{0}. Lifting exists iff f_* (π1(V)) ⊆ p_* (π1(E)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely, for the square map p, p_*(π1) corresponds to 2Z; hence for every loop γ in V we require the winding number of f∘γ around 0 to be even. This yields the integral condition involving (1/(2πi)) ∮ f'/f dz ∈ nZ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of holomorphic nth roots (Theorem 33.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : U → C be holomorphic. Then f has a holomorphic nth root if and only if (1/(2πi)) ∮_γ f'/f dz ∈ nZ for every contour γ in U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent topological condition: all winding numbers of f around 0 (for loops in U avoiding zeros) must be multiples of n. Handle zeros separately by local square-root choices; global obstruction is the monodromy encoded by f'/f integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of logarithms (Theorem 33.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : U → C be holomorphic. Then f has a logarithm iff (1/(2πi)) ∮_γ f'/f dz = 0 for every contour γ in U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: f must be zero-free and have trivial monodromy (no net winding around 0) on every loop. This follows from viewing exp: C → C\{0} as the universal cover so p_*(π1) is trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonvanishing on simply connected domains implies existence of logs and roots (Corollary 33.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : Ω → C be continuous where Ω is simply connected. If f(z) ≠ 0 for every z ∈ Ω, then f has both a logarithm and holomorphic nth root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because simply connected domain kills π1 obstructions: trivial winding numbers ensure the conditions in Theorems 33.3.2 and 33.4.2 are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branch-cut/principal branch construction for log and nth root (Theorem 33.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist holomorphic functions log : C \ (−∞,0] → C and n√· : C \ (−∞,0] → C satisfying the usual properties (principal branches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing a branch cut (e.g., remove negative real axis) prevents loops around 0 and removes monodromy; principal branch chooses imaginary part of log in (−π,π] and gives canonical choices (Log z). Many other branches possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/computational application: counting zeros numerically
rubrics_metrics.description: By evaluating (1/(2πi)) ∮_γ f'/f numerically on chosen circles γ, one can determine the number of zeros inside a region even with rounding error because the integral is close to an integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in numerical investigations (e.g., verifying zeros of the Riemann zeta function) — integral's integer nature makes it robust to small numerical perturbations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument-principle geometric viewpoint (winding of f∘γ)
rubrics_metrics.description: The integral (1/(2πi)) ∮_γ f'/f dz equals the winding number I(f∘γ,0), i.e., how many times f∘γ winds around the origin; this is the geometric content of the argument principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: formally d/dz log f = f'/f and integrating d log f over γ records the multivalued jump in log, which counts net turns of f(γ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and counterexamples to meromorphicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples demonstrating meromorphic functions (e.g., (z+1)/sin z, 1/sin z, rational functions) and a non-meromorphic example (1/sin(1/z) at 0) illustrating that a point without a Laurent series neighborhood is not a pole and so may prevent meromorphic extension over that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to test definitions: identify poles, compute residues and orders, and check Laurent expansions; note that accumulation points of poles (non-isolated) break meromorphicity at an accumulation point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Cauchy-Goursat and Cauchy integral formula in residue arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy-Goursat (integral of holomorphic function over closed loop in simply connected domain is zero) is the key input used repeatedly (e.g., to show integral of holomorphic part g vanishes in residue theorem and in deriving Cauchy's integral formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 31.7.6 explicitly: Cauchy-Goursat is used in proof of Cauchy's integral formula. Many contour arguments rely on vanishing integrals of holomorphic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Log/roots obstruction phrased as monodromy/winding integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Global existence of single-valued holomorphic logarithm or nth root is obstructed precisely by the monodromy around loops; the obstruction is measured by (1/(2πi)) ∮ f'/f dz which must be 0 (for log) or an n-multiple (for nth root) for all loops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combines algebraic-topological viewpoint (lifting to covering spaces) with analytic integrals (logarithmic derivative). It gives a practical test for existence of branches.
